points.en: Biblical precedent: God called ordinary working people (Amos, Moses, Paul, Philip) to proclaim His word, so lack of professional standing is no barrier.
Historical pattern: lay preachers (Methodist revival, frontier farmers, Moody) advanced the work of God when no professionals were available.
Priesthood of all believers: the whole church is a priesthood, so a believer with the gift of speech may use it to build up the church.
Lay preachers can be effective, and there have never been enough ordained clergy to meet every preaching need.
God demands preparation: the preacher is a steward of the Bible whose authority depends on how faithfully he has studied the text (2 Timothy 2:15).
The task demands it: congregations come asking whether there is a word from the Lord, and the preacher has no right to give them anything else.
Preparation removes the fear of having nothing to say and gives the sermon a direction so it does not wander.
Preparation does not compete with the Spirit; it gives Him a week to shape the preacher's thoughts before he preaches.
Identifies a one-word summary, a summary verse and a theme that fit Jonah's message.
Gives a three-point outline drawn from the book of Jonah that develops the chosen theme.
Explains why preaching a whole book suits the occasion: one sweeping overview of a short book in a single message.
The three points are worded in parallel form.
States the idea of 1 Corinthians 13 in one sentence (love).
Forms a complete probing question by joining the idea with one of the interrogatives (who, which, what, why, when, where, how, how much).
Gives a three-point outline drawn from the chapter, with the points parallel in form.
Gives a Scripture reference supporting each point.
Gives a four-point outline following Barclay's four implications of bondservant: absolute obedience, humility, loyalty and pride.
Teaches the idea in plain words such as servant or bondservant rather than using the Greek word in the lesson.
Each point is tied to what it means for a believer to belong to Christ as His bondservant.
The parable approach (Good Samaritan) is a focused story, an earthly story with a heavenly meaning, built around one main truth.
The character approach (Barnabas) is a study of a person's life that draws several pastoral lessons from it.
Chooses one approach for teenagers and gives a reasoned justification.
Notes that people are naturally interested in the lives of others, so a character can draw teenagers in.
Advantage: consecutive preaching covers the whole counsel of God rather than only the preacher's favorite passages.
Advantage: much of the preparation is done in advance through the preaching analysis of the book.
Disadvantage: it requires discipline, because the preacher must follow the text rather than his own moods.
Offers a further advantage or disadvantage, such as continuity for hearers or difficulty addressing topical needs.
The text and the sermon theme do not match: Psalm 142:4 is David's lament that no one cared for his soul, not a passage about caring for lost souls.
Proposes a different text that really speaks of God's concern for the lost (for example Luke 19:10).
The principle: the theme of the text and the theme of the sermon must be the same, or the text becomes only a perch for the preacher's own ideas.
Foundation is the text, the Word of God that gives stability; the entryway is the introduction, which leads people in and should be small.
Support beams are the divisions, which hold up the structure and are not meant to be admired; windows are the illustrations, which let light in.
The exit is the conclusion.
Neglecting any part produces a matching fault in the sermon, for example no text means the preacher's own ideas, or an oversized introduction.
Names three of the seven methods: whole book, chapter, theme, word, miracle or parable, character, consecutive analysis.
Gives a concrete Biblical example for each chosen method.
Explains an occasion where each chosen method would be the best choice, matching the method's strength.
Briefly describes what each chosen method involves.
